# Integer execution unit {#sec-ieu .unnumbered}

## Goal for this week

- Know what the integer execution unit (IEU) does, and which instructions
  it executes
- Read the IEU interface: the handshake with Decode and Memory, the
  operands and controls from Decode, the forwarding inputs and the redirect
- Build the IEU from generic blocks: the D/E pipeline registers, the
  forwarding and operand multiplexers, the ALU and the branch logic
- Understand why the operand registers must be refreshed with forwarded
  values while the stage waits

## Introduction

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- Execute is the **heart of the CPU**: here the instruction does its work
- Everything before it prepares operands, everything after it stores results
- HIPV implements **RV32I** only: no multiply/divide, no floating point
- Every operation finishes in **one cycle**
- Executed in the IEU:
  - arithmetic and logic: `add`, `sub`, `and`, `or`, `xor`, shifts, compares
  - immediates: `addi`, `andi`, …, `lui`, `auipc`
  - memory addresses for loads and stores: `rs1 + imm`
  - branches: `beq`, `bne`, `blt`, `bge`, `bltu`, `bgeu`
  - jumps: `jal`, `jalr`
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The execution stage is the heart of every CPU. It is the place where an
instruction actually does its work: two numbers are added, compared or
shifted, a memory address is computed, a branch decides where the program
goes next. The stages before it only prepare this moment. Fetch brings the
instruction, Decode works out what it means and reads its operands. The
stages after it only finish the job. Memory performs the access whose
address Execute has computed, and Writeback stores the result in the
register file.

HIPV implements the base integer instruction set of RISC-V, **RV32I**. It
has no multiplication and division (the M extension) and no floating point,
so every operation the IEU performs is simple enough to finish in a single
clock cycle. The IEU handles three kinds of work:

- **Arithmetic and logic.** The register–register instructions `add`, `sub`,
  `sll`, `slt`, `sltu`, `xor`, `srl`, `sra`, `or` and `and`, and their
  register–immediate forms `addi`, `slli`, `slti`, `sltiu`, `xori`, `srli`,
  `srai`, `ori` and `andi`. The two upper-immediate instructions `lui` and
  `auipc` are also additions in the ALU.
- **Address calculation.** Loads and stores address memory as `rs1 + imm`.
  The IEU computes this sum, and the Memory stage uses it.
- **Control flow.** The six conditional branches `beq`, `bne`, `blt`, `bge`,
  `bltu` and `bgeu`, and the two jumps `jal` and `jalr`. The IEU decides
  whether the branch is taken, computes the target, and tells Fetch to
  continue from there.
:::

## Interface of the IEU

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
| Group | Signals |
|---|---|
| Handshake with Decode | `ValidD` (in), `ReadyE` (out) |
| From Decode | operands, register numbers, controls (`…D`) |
| Forwarding | `ForwardAE`, `ForwardBE`, `ForwardDataM`, `ResultW` (in) |
| Redirect to Fetch and Decode | `PCSrcE`, `PCTargetE` (out) |
| Handshake with Memory | `ValidE` (out), `ReadyM` (in) |
| To Memory | `ALUResultE`, `WriteDataE`, `PCPlus4E`, `RdE`, controls (out) |
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The ports of the IEU fall into five groups: the handshake with Decode
together with everything Decode has produced, the forwarding inputs, the
redirect to Fetch and Decode, and the handshake with the Memory stage
together with the stage outputs. As before, the suffix of each name says
which stage the signal belongs to.

```systemverilog
module ieu (input  logic        clk, reset,
            // handshake with the Decode stage
            input  logic        ValidD,
            output logic        ReadyE,
            // inputs from Decode
            input  logic [31:0] RD1D, RD2D, ImmExtD, PCD, PCPlus4D,
            input  logic [4:0]  Rs1D, Rs2D, RdD,
            input  logic [2:0]  Funct3D,
            input  logic        RegWriteD, MemWriteD, BranchD, JumpD, JalrD,
            input  logic [1:0]  ResultSrcD, ALUSrcAD,
            input  logic        ALUSrcBD,
            input  logic [3:0]  ALUControlD,
            // forwarding (from the hazard unit and later stages)
            input  logic [1:0]  ForwardAE, ForwardBE,
            input  logic [31:0] ForwardDataM, ResultW,
            // redirect to Fetch/Decode
            output logic        PCSrcE,
            output logic [31:0] PCTargetE,
            // handshake with the Memory stage
            output logic        ValidE,
            input  logic        ReadyM,
            // stage outputs to Memory
            output logic [31:0] ALUResultE, WriteDataE, PCPlus4E,
            output logic [4:0]  RdE,
            output logic [4:0]  Rs1E, Rs2E,
            output logic [2:0]  Funct3E,
            output logic        RegWriteE, MemWriteE,
            output logic [1:0]  ResultSrcE);
```
:::

### Handshake with Decode

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- `ValidD`: Decode offers a decoded instruction
- `ReadyE`: Execute can accept it
- Transfer at the edge where **both** are 1
- The same valid/ready pair as between Fetch and Decode
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The IEU receives instructions from Decode over the same valid/ready
handshake that connects Fetch and Decode (@sec-handshake). `ValidD`
says that Decode offers a decoded instruction, and `ReadyE` says that
Execute can accept it. The instruction moves into Execute at a clock edge
where both are high. How `ReadyE` is computed is the subject of
@sec-ieu-handshake.
:::

### Signals from Decode

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
| Group | Signals | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| ALU operation | `ALUControlD`, `ALUSrcAD`, `ALUSrcBD` | what the ALU computes, from which operands |
| Branches and jumps | `BranchD`, `JumpD`, `JalrD`, `Funct3D` | whether and where to redirect |
| Later stages | `MemWriteD`, `ResultSrcD`, `RegWriteD`, `RdD` | passed on to Memory and Writeback |
| Operands | `RD1D`, `RD2D`, `ImmExtD`, `PCD`, `PCPlus4D` | the data |
| Register numbers | `Rs1D`, `Rs2D` | the forwarding decision |
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Decode hands the IEU everything the instruction needs, already worked out.
The signals fall into five groups:

| Group | Signals | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| ALU operation | `ALUControlD`, `ALUSrcAD`, `ALUSrcBD` | what the ALU computes, and from which operands |
| Branches and jumps | `BranchD`, `JumpD`, `JalrD`, `Funct3D` | whether to redirect, and where |
| Later stages | `MemWriteD`, `ResultSrcD`, `RegWriteD`, `RdD` | not used here, passed on to Memory and Writeback |
| Operands | `RD1D`, `RD2D`, `ImmExtD`, `PCD`, `PCPlus4D` | the data to compute with |
| Register numbers | `Rs1D`, `Rs2D` | the forwarding decision in the hazard unit |

`Funct3D` serves two purposes. For a branch it selects the condition
(`beq`, `blt`, …), and for a load or store it selects the access size,
which is why it also travels on to the Memory stage. The control signals
for later stages pass through the IEU unchanged: Execute stores them in its
pipeline registers and hands them on together with its result.
:::

### Forwarding inputs

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- `ForwardDataM`: the result of the instruction in Memory
- `ResultW`: the result of the instruction in Writeback
- `ForwardAE`, `ForwardBE`: from the hazard unit, which value to use for
  operand A and B
- `Rs1E`, `Rs2E` go out to the hazard unit for the comparison
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
An operand read from the register file in Decode can be out of date. The
instruction that produces it may still be in the Memory or Writeback stage,
with its result computed but not yet written to the register file. The IEU
therefore receives the two newest results in the pipeline:

- `ForwardDataM`, the result of the instruction in the Memory stage. For a
  load this is the loaded data, otherwise the ALU result.
- `ResultW`, the result of the instruction in the Writeback stage.

The hazard unit decides which of the values the IEU should use, and tells
it with two 2-bit selects, `ForwardAE` for operand A and `ForwardBE` for
operand B. For that decision it needs to know which registers the
instruction in Execute reads, so the IEU exports `Rs1E` and `Rs2E`.
:::

### Redirect to Fetch and Decode

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- `PCSrcE`: 1 = jump or taken branch
- `PCTargetE`: the target address
- Fetch loads the PC with the target, Decode flushes its instruction
- One-cycle pulse, in the cycle the branch leaves Execute
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Branches and jumps are resolved here, so the IEU drives the redirect that
we met from the receiving side in the [IFU chapter](06b-ifu.qmd): `PCSrcE`
says that a jump or a taken branch has occurred, and `PCTargetE` carries the
target address. Fetch loads its PC with the target, and Decode throws away
the instruction it holds, which was fetched from the wrong path.
:::

### Handshake and outputs to Memory

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- `ValidE` (out), `ReadyM` (in): the next handshake down the pipeline
- `ALUResultE`: the result, or the memory address
- `WriteDataE`: the store data (forwarded `rs2`)
- `PCPlus4E`: the return address of `jal`/`jalr`
- `RdE`, `Funct3E`, `RegWriteE`, `MemWriteE`, `ResultSrcE`: passed on
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Towards the Memory stage, the IEU is the sender: `ValidE` says that its
outputs hold a valid instruction, and `ReadyM` says that the Memory stage
can take it. The outputs are the ALU result `ALUResultE`, which is either
the result of an arithmetic instruction or the address of a load or store,
the store data `WriteDataE`, the return address `PCPlus4E` for `jal` and
`jalr`, and the controls that the later stages still need.
:::

## Structure of the IEU

![The IEU: the handshake logic and the D/E pipeline registers, the forwarding multiplexers (`fwdamux`, `fwdbmux`), the operand multiplexers (`srcamux`, `srcbmux`), the ALU, and the branch logic (`branchcmp`, `targetadd`, `targetmux`) that drives the redirect.](../images/blocks/ieu.svg){#fig-ieu}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- **Handshake and pipeline registers**: accept the instruction from Decode
- **Forwarding**: `fwdamux`, `fwdbmux`, the newest value of each register
- **ALU**: `srcamux`, `srcbmux`, `alu`
- **Jumps and branches**: `branchcmp`, `targetadd`, `targetmux`, `PCSrcE`
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
@fig-ieu shows the IEU. Data flows from left to right through four parts,
and the rest of the chapter takes them one at a time:

1. the **handshake logic and the pipeline registers**, which accept the
   instruction from Decode and hold it while it executes;
2. the **forwarding multiplexers**, which replace an out-of-date register
   operand with a newer value from the Memory or Writeback stage;
3. the **ALU** with its two operand multiplexers, which computes the
   result;
4. the **jump mechanism**, which evaluates the branch condition, computes
   the target and drives the redirect.
:::

## Handshake logic and pipeline registers {#sec-ieu-handshake}

![The handshake logic of the IEU. `ReadyE` tells Decode that Execute can take a new instruction, `EnDE` loads the D/E registers, and `validreg` remembers whether the stage holds a valid instruction.](../images/blocks/ieu-handshake.svg){#fig-ieu-handshake}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
  // D/E handshake: accept when the stage is empty or being drained
  assign ReadyE = ~ValidEReg | ReadyM;
  assign EnDE   = ValidD & ReadyE;
  assign ValidE = ValidEReg;

  // D/E valid bit
  always_ff @(posedge clk)
    if (reset) ValidEReg <= 1'b0;
    else if (ReadyE) ValidEReg <= ValidD;
```

- `ReadyE`: stage empty, **or** its instruction leaves this cycle
- `EnDE`: an instruction moves from Decode into Execute
- `ValidEReg`: the stage holds a valid instruction
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The handshake logic is the same as in Decode (@fig-idu-handshake), with one
difference: Decode
also listens to `PCSrcE` and flushes its instruction on a redirect, while
Execute is never flushed. A branch is resolved in Execute, so everything
that is wrong about it lies *behind* it, in Fetch and Decode. The branch
itself is correct and continues to the Memory stage like any other
instruction.

```systemverilog
  // D/E handshake: accept when the stage is empty or being drained
  assign ReadyE = ~ValidEReg | ReadyM;
  assign EnDE   = ValidD & ReadyE;
  assign ValidE = ValidEReg;

  // D/E valid bit
  always_ff @(posedge clk)
    if (reset) ValidEReg <= 1'b0;
    else if (ReadyE) ValidEReg <= ValidD;
```

Three signals make up the handshake (@fig-ieu-handshake):

- `ValidEReg` is the **valid bit** of the stage, a one-bit register that
  says whether the stage holds a valid instruction or a bubble. It is reset
  to 0, an empty stage. Whenever the stage can accept a new instruction, it
  takes over `ValidD`: it becomes 1 if Decode delivers an instruction, and
  0, a bubble, if Decode has nothing to offer. It is also the stage output
  `ValidE`.
- `ReadyE` tells Decode that Execute can accept a new instruction. That is
  the case when the stage is empty (`~ValidEReg`), or when the instruction
  it holds leaves at this very edge because the Memory stage is ready to
  take it (`ReadyM`). The second term is what lets the pipeline move one
  instruction per cycle: the place is freed and refilled at the same edge.
  When the Memory stage stalls, `ReadyE` drops, and the stall propagates
  backwards to Decode and Fetch.
- `EnDE` is the transfer itself: Decode offers an instruction (`ValidD`)
  and Execute accepts it (`ReadyE`). It is the enable of the pipeline
  registers.
:::

### The D/E pipeline registers

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
  flopenr #(32) rd1reg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE | HoldE), .D(RD1NextE), .Q(RD1E));
  flopenr #(32) rd2reg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE | HoldE), .D(RD2NextE), .Q(RD2E));
  flopenr #(32) immreg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE), .D(ImmExtD), .Q(ImmExtE));
  flopenr #(32) pcreg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE), .D(PCD), .Q(PCE));
  flopenr #(32) pcplus4reg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE), .D(PCPlus4D), .Q(PCPlus4E));
  flopenr #(15) regsreg(...  {Rs1D, Rs2D, RdD} ...);
  flopenr #(3)  funct3reg(... Funct3D ...);
  flopenr #(14) ctrlreg(...  all control signals ...);
```

- Loaded on `EnDE`, at the transfer from Decode
- Hold their value while the instruction waits in Execute
- Exception: `rd1reg`, `rd2reg` (next section)
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The pipeline registers store everything Decode has produced for the
instruction, and they are loaded at the transfer, on `EnDE`. Between
transfers they hold their value, so the instruction stays in Execute,
with all its operands and controls stable, for as long as the Memory stage
makes it wait. All of them are the generic `flopenr`, with the width of
the signals they store:

```systemverilog
  flopenr #(32) rd1reg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE | HoldE), .D(RD1NextE), .Q(RD1E));
  flopenr #(32) rd2reg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE | HoldE), .D(RD2NextE), .Q(RD2E));
  flopenr #(32) immreg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE), .D(ImmExtD), .Q(ImmExtE));
  flopenr #(32) pcreg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE), .D(PCD), .Q(PCE));
  flopenr #(32) pcplus4reg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE), .D(PCPlus4D), .Q(PCPlus4E));
  flopenr #(15) regsreg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE),
                        .D({Rs1D, Rs2D, RdD}), .Q({Rs1E, Rs2E, RdE}));
  flopenr #(3)  funct3reg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE), .D(Funct3D), .Q(Funct3E));
  flopenr #(14) ctrlreg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE),
                        .D({RegWriteD, MemWriteD, BranchD, JumpD, JalrD, ResultSrcD,
                            ALUSrcAD, ALUSrcBD, ALUControlD}),
                        .Q({RegWriteE, MemWriteE, BranchE, JumpE, JalrE, ResultSrcE,
                            ALUSrcAE, ALUSrcBE, ALUControlE}));
```

Signals that belong together share one register: the three register
numbers in `regsreg`, and all fourteen control bits in `ctrlreg`. The
concatenation `{…}` packs them into one vector on the input and unpacks
them on the output. Only the two register operands, in `rd1reg` and
`rd2reg`, have a different input and enable. They are the subject of
@sec-ieu-refresh.
:::

## Forwarding

![Forwarding for operand A. The hazard unit compares the register numbers and drives `ForwardAE`; `fwdamux` in the IEU selects the value, `FwdAE`.](../images/blocks/forwarding.svg){#fig-ieu-forwarding}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
  // forwarding muxes: register operand / ResultW / ForwardDataM
  mux3 #(32) fwdamux(.D0(RD1E), .D1(ResultW), .D2(ForwardDataM), .S(ForwardAE), .Y(FwdAE));
  mux3 #(32) fwdbmux(.D0(RD2E), .D1(ResultW), .D2(ForwardDataM), .S(ForwardBE), .Y(WriteDataE));
```

| `ForwardAE` | Name | Value used |
|---|---|---|
| `00` | `FWD_RF` | `RD1E`, read from the register file in Decode |
| `01` | `FWD_WB` | `ResultW`, from the Writeback stage |
| `10` | `FWD_MEM` | `ForwardDataM`, from the Memory stage |
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The two register operands pass through a forwarding multiplexer each,
`fwdamux` for operand A (`rs1`) and `fwdbmux` for operand B (`rs2`). Both
are three-input multiplexers, the generic `mux3`:

```systemverilog
module mux3 #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] D0, D1, D2,
  input  logic [1:0]       S,
  output logic [WIDTH-1:0] Y);

  assign Y = (S == 2'b10) ? D2 : (S == 2'b01) ? D1 : D0;

endmodule
```

The nested conditional operator checks `S` against the two encodings of
`D2` and `D1`, and falls back to `D0` for everything else, including the
unused `11`. In the IEU, the two instances choose between three versions of
the same register:

```systemverilog
  // forwarding muxes: register operand / ResultW / ForwardDataM
  mux3 #(32) fwdamux(.D0(RD1E), .D1(ResultW), .D2(ForwardDataM), .S(ForwardAE), .Y(FwdAE));
  mux3 #(32) fwdbmux(.D0(RD2E), .D1(ResultW), .D2(ForwardDataM), .S(ForwardBE), .Y(WriteDataE));
```

- `D0` is the value from the D/E pipeline register, `RD1E` or `RD2E`, as it
  was read from the register file in Decode;
- `D1` is `ResultW`, the result of the instruction in the Writeback stage;
- `D2` is `ForwardDataM`, the result of the instruction in the Memory
  stage.

The selects come from the hazard unit (@fig-ieu-forwarding). Their three
values are named in the package `hipv_pkg`, so that the code says what a
select means rather than which bits it has:

```systemverilog
  // forwarding select (ForwardAE / ForwardBE, from the hazard unit)
  localparam logic [1:0] FWD_RF  = 2'b00;  // register operand from D/E register
  localparam logic [1:0] FWD_WB  = 2'b01;  // ResultW from the Writeback stage
  localparam logic [1:0] FWD_MEM = 2'b10;  // ForwardDataM from the Memory stage
```

The hazard unit selects `FWD_MEM` when the instruction in the Memory stage
writes the register the operand reads, `FWD_WB` when the instruction in
Writeback does, and `FWD_RF` otherwise. If both match, the Memory stage
wins, because it holds the younger instruction and therefore the newer
value. The details of that decision belong to the
[chapter on hazards](07-pipeline-hazards.qmd). The IEU only carries it out.

The outputs of the two multiplexers are the true values of `rs1` and
`rs2`, and every later block in the IEU uses them instead of `RD1E` and
`RD2E`. `FwdAE` goes to the ALU operand multiplexer and to the branch
comparator. `WriteDataE` goes to the same two places, and on to the Memory
stage as the store data, which is where its name comes from.
:::

### Refreshing the operands with forwarded values {#sec-ieu-refresh}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- An instruction can **wait** in Execute: the Memory stage is not ready
- Meanwhile its producer can **leave** Writeback, and is no longer
  forwarded
- `RD1E` was read in Decode, **before** the producer wrote it: stale
- If we keep only the value from Decode, the forwarded value is **lost**

```
lw   x5, 0(x10)    # slow memory: the next instructions bunch up
addi x1, x0, 77    # producer of x1
sw   x5, 4(x10)    # holds the Memory stage
add  x3, x1, x0    # waits in Execute; x1 forwarded from W for one cycle only
```
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Forwarding as described so far has a gap. An instruction does not always
spend just one cycle in Execute. When the Memory stage is busy with a slow
load or store, `ReadyM` is low, and the instruction in Execute has to wait.
The forwarded value, however, is available only as long as its producer is
in the Memory or Writeback stage. If the producer leaves Writeback while
the consumer is still waiting, nothing forwards the value any more. The
operand in the pipeline register does not help either: it was read from
the register file in Decode, *before* the producer wrote it, so it is
stale.

Consider this sequence on a slow data memory:

```
lw   x5, 0(x10)    # slow memory: the next instructions bunch up
addi x1, x0, 77    # producer of x1
sw   x5, 4(x10)    # holds the Memory stage
add  x3, x1, x0    # waits in Execute; x1 forwarded from W for one cycle only
```

When `addi` reaches Writeback, `sw` is in the Memory stage and `add` in
Execute. The hazard unit sees that `add` reads `x1` and `addi` writes it,
and selects `FWD_WB`. But `sw` holds the Memory stage for several cycles,
so `add` cannot leave Execute. In the next cycle `addi` has left the
pipeline, the hazard unit falls back to `FWD_RF`, and `fwdamux` delivers
`RD1E`, the old value of `x1` read in Decode. When `add` finally executes,
it computes with the wrong operand.

The solution is to not let the forwarded value go: as long as the
instruction waits, the operand register is reloaded with the output of the
forwarding multiplexer. This is a feedback loop from `fwdamux` back to the
input of `rd1reg`, and the same from `fwdbmux` to `rd2reg`.
:::

### The refresh loop in SystemVerilog

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
  assign HoldE = ValidEReg & ~ReadyM;
  mux2 #(32) rd1mux(.D0(FwdAE), .D1(RD1D), .S(EnDE), .Y(RD1NextE));
  mux2 #(32) rd2mux(.D0(WriteDataE), .D1(RD2D), .S(EnDE), .Y(RD2NextE));
  flopenr #(32) rd1reg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE | HoldE), .D(RD1NextE), .Q(RD1E));
  flopenr #(32) rd2reg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE | HoldE), .D(RD2NextE), .Q(RD2E));
```

| `EnDE` | `HoldE` | `rd1reg` loads |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | `RD1D`: a new instruction from Decode |
| 0 | 1 | `FwdAE`: refresh while the instruction waits |
| 0 | 0 | nothing: the stage is empty or being drained |
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
  // While an instruction waits in E, refresh its register operands with
  // the forwarded values: the producer can retire from W (and stop being
  // forwarded) before this instruction leaves E.
  assign HoldE = ValidEReg & ~ReadyM;
  mux2 #(32) rd1mux(.D0(FwdAE), .D1(RD1D), .S(EnDE), .Y(RD1NextE));
  mux2 #(32) rd2mux(.D0(WriteDataE), .D1(RD2D), .S(EnDE), .Y(RD2NextE));
  flopenr #(32) rd1reg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE | HoldE), .D(RD1NextE), .Q(RD1E));
  flopenr #(32) rd2reg(.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(EnDE | HoldE), .D(RD2NextE), .Q(RD2E));
```

This code describes the datapath in @fig-ieu-holde, shown for operand A.
Operand B is built the same way, with `rd2mux`, `rd2reg` and `fwdbmux`.
:::

![The refresh loop for operand A. `rd1mux` chooses between the operand from Decode and the forwarded value `FwdAE`; `rd1reg` is loaded on a transfer (`EnDE`) and in every cycle the instruction waits (`HoldE`).](../images/blocks/holde.svg){#fig-ieu-holde}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- `HoldE`: valid instruction in Execute, Memory stage **not ready**
- `HoldE = ~ReadyE`: never at the same time as `EnDE`
- Each waiting cycle stores whatever `fwdamux` selects: `ResultW`,
  `ForwardDataM`, or its own value
- The last forwarded value before the producer leaves is **kept**
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The datapath has three parts:

- **`rd1mux`** chooses what will be stored in `rd1reg`.
  - When `EnDE = 1`, a new instruction enters Execute, and the register
    stores its operand from Decode, `RD1D`.
  - When `EnDE = 0`, no instruction enters, and the register stores the
    output of the forwarding multiplexer, `FwdAE`.
- **`rd1reg`** stores the operand. Its enable is `EnDE | HoldE`, so it
  loads in two situations: at the transfer from Decode, and in every cycle
  in which the stage is on hold. `HoldE = ValidEReg & ~ReadyM` says that the
  stage holds a valid instruction, but the Memory stage is not ready to
  take it, so the instruction has to wait.
- **`fwdamux`** is the same forwarding multiplexer as before. Through the
  loop it also decides what `rd1reg` stores while the stage is on hold:
  `ForwardDataM`, `ResultW`, or, with `FWD_RF`, the register's own value,
  which simply keeps it.

`HoldE` and `EnDE` are never high at the same time. Substituting `ReadyE`
shows that `HoldE` is exactly its complement, `ValidEReg & ~ReadyM =
~(~ValidEReg | ReadyM) = ~ReadyE`: the stage is on hold precisely when it
cannot accept a new instruction, and then `EnDE` is 0. The register
therefore never has to choose between a new operand and a refresh, and
`EnDE` alone is a sufficient select for `rd1mux`. When both are 0, the
stage is empty, or its instruction is leaving without a successor, and the
register keeps a value that nobody uses.

Back to the example. In the cycle in which `addi` is in Writeback, `add` is
on hold, and `fwdamux` delivers `ResultW = 77`. At the end of the cycle
`rd1reg` stores 77. In the next cycle `addi` is gone and the hazard unit
selects `FWD_RF`, but `RD1E` now *is* 77, and the loop keeps it there until
`add` leaves Execute.

The refresh is harmless when the forwarded value is not ready yet. If the
producer is a load still waiting for its data, `ForwardDataM` carries
garbage, and `rd1reg` stores it. But while the load is in the Memory stage,
`ReadyM` is low, so the consumer is on hold and does not use the garbage.
When the data is there, `ReadyM` rises, `ForwardDataM` carries the loaded
value, and the consumer leaves Execute computing with it, straight from
`fwdamux`. This is why HIPV needs no special load-use stall: the elastic
handshake and the refresh loop together cover that case.
:::

## The ALU

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- The **workhorse** of the CPU: one combinational block, all operations
- Two 32-bit operands `A`, `B` → one 32-bit result `Y`
- `ALUControl` (4 bits) selects one of ten operations
- No clock, no state: the result is ready within the same cycle
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The arithmetic-logic unit (ALU) is the workhorse of every CPU. It is a
purely combinational block: it takes two operands, computes one of a fixed
set of operations on them, and produces a result, all within one clock
cycle and without any state of its own. Which operation it computes is
chosen by a control input. Most instructions of a program pass through it,
not only the arithmetic ones. A load or store uses it for the address, and
`jalr` for the jump target.

The ALU of HIPV has two 32-bit operands, `A` and `B`, a 4-bit control
`ALUControl`, and a 32-bit result `Y`. It implements the ten operations
that RV32I needs. Inside, it is simply a separate circuit for each
operation (an adder, a subtractor, a shifter, a comparator, the bitwise
gates), followed by a large multiplexer that selects one result.
:::

### Operands of the ALU

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
| `ALUSrcAE` | `SrcAE` | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `00` `SRCA_RF` | `FwdAE` (`rs1`) | `add x3, x1, x2`, `lw x3, 8(x1)` |
| `01` `SRCA_PC` | `PCE` | `auipc x5, 0x12` → `x5 = PC + 0x12000` |
| `10` `SRCA_ZERO` | 0 | `lui x5, 0x12` → `x5 = 0 + 0x12000` |

| `ALUSrcBE` | `SrcBE` | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `WriteDataE` (`rs2`) | `add x3, x1, x2` |
| 1 | `ImmExtE` | `addi x3, x1, 5`, `lw x3, 8(x1)`, `sw x3, 8(x1)` |
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The operands of the ALU come from two multiplexers, one per operand:

```systemverilog
  // ALU operand selection: A = rs1/PC/zero, B = rs2/immediate
  mux3 #(32) srcamux(.D0(FwdAE), .D1(PCE), .D2(32'b0), .S(ALUSrcAE), .Y(SrcAE));
  mux2 #(32) srcbmux(.D0(WriteDataE), .D1(ImmExtE), .S(ALUSrcBE), .Y(SrcBE));
```

Operand A, `SrcAE`, is selected by `ALUSrcAE` from three sources:

| `ALUSrcAE` | `SrcAE` | Used by | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `00` `SRCA_RF` | `FwdAE`, the forwarded `rs1` | almost all instructions | `add x3, x1, x2`; `lw x3, 8(x1)` |
| `01` `SRCA_PC` | `PCE`, the address of the instruction | `auipc` | `auipc x5, 0x12` gives `x5 = PC + 0x12000` |
| `10` `SRCA_ZERO` | 0 | `lui` | `lui x5, 0x12` gives `x5 = 0 + 0x12000` |

Selecting zero for `lui` is a small trick. `lui` only has to copy its
immediate into the destination register, and adding it to zero does that
with the ALU's ordinary `ADD`, without a separate path to the output.

Operand B, `SrcBE`, is selected by `ALUSrcBE` from two sources:

| `ALUSrcBE` | `SrcBE` | Used by | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `WriteDataE`, the forwarded `rs2` | register–register instructions | `add x3, x1, x2` |
| 1 | `ImmExtE`, the extended immediate | register–immediate, loads, stores, `lui`, `auipc`, `jalr` | `addi x3, x1, 5`; `sw x3, 8(x1)` |

Both multiplexers come after the forwarding multiplexers, so whenever the
ALU uses a register, it uses its forwarded value.
:::

### The ALU in SystemVerilog

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module alu (input  logic [31:0] A, B,
            input  logic [3:0]  ALUControl,
            output logic [31:0] Y);

  import hipv_pkg::*;

  always_comb
    case (ALUControl)
      ALU_ADD:  Y = A + B;
      ALU_SUB:  Y = A - B;
      ALU_SLL:  Y = A << B[4:0];
      ALU_SLT:  Y = {31'b0, $signed(A) < $signed(B)};
      ALU_SLTU: Y = {31'b0, A < B};
      ALU_XOR:  Y = A ^ B;
      ALU_SRL:  Y = A >> B[4:0];
      ALU_SRA:  Y = $unsigned($signed(A) >>> B[4:0]);
      ALU_OR:   Y = A | B;
      ALU_AND:  Y = A & B;
      default:  Y = 32'b0;
    endcase

endmodule
```
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The ALU is one of the few behavioral blocks of the core. It is a single
`case` over `ALUControl`, inside `always_comb`:

```systemverilog
module alu (input  logic [31:0] A, B,
            input  logic [3:0]  ALUControl,
            output logic [31:0] Y);

  import hipv_pkg::*;

  always_comb
    case (ALUControl)
      ALU_ADD:  Y = A + B;
      ALU_SUB:  Y = A - B;
      ALU_SLL:  Y = A << B[4:0];
      ALU_SLT:  Y = {31'b0, $signed(A) < $signed(B)};
      ALU_SLTU: Y = {31'b0, A < B};
      ALU_XOR:  Y = A ^ B;
      ALU_SRL:  Y = A >> B[4:0];
      ALU_SRA:  Y = $unsigned($signed(A) >>> B[4:0]);
      ALU_OR:   Y = A | B;
      ALU_AND:  Y = A & B;
      default:  Y = 32'b0;
    endcase

endmodule
```

The operation codes `ALU_ADD` to `ALU_AND` are the constants 0 to 9 from
`hipv_pkg`, imported at the top of the module. Decode produces the same
names, so the two ends always agree on the encoding. A few lines deserve a
closer look:

- **Shifts** use only the lowest five bits of `B`, because a 32-bit value
  can be shifted by at most 31 places. This also makes the immediate shifts
  work: in `srai`, bit 10 of the immediate distinguishes it from `srli`,
  but it lies outside `B[4:0]` and does not disturb the shift amount.
- **Signed and unsigned.** SystemVerilog treats a `logic` vector as
  unsigned. `slt` and `sltu` compare the same bits, but `slt` first
  reinterprets them with `$signed`, so that `0xFFFFFFFF` counts as −1 and
  not as 4 294 967 295. The comparison gives one bit, and `{31'b0, …}`
  extends it to the 32-bit result 0 or 1.
- **Arithmetic shift.** `>>>` fills the vacated bits with copies of the
  sign bit only if its operand is signed, so `A` is converted with
  `$signed`, and the result is converted back with `$unsigned` before it is
  assigned to `Y`.
- **`default`** covers the six unused codes 10 to 15. Without it, `Y` would
  not be assigned for them, and `always_comb` would infer a latch
  (see the chapter on [designing with SystemVerilog](05-sv-design.qmd)).

In the IEU, the ALU is a single instance, and its result is the stage
output `ALUResultE`:

```systemverilog
  alu alu(.A(SrcAE), .B(SrcBE), .ALUControl(ALUControlE), .Y(ALUResultE));
```

You have built this block before. In the second lab exercise you
implemented a "dummy" 4-bit ALU with a 3-bit `alu_control`, using operators,
intermediate signals and nested conditionals. The ALU of HIPV is the same
idea at full size. The operands are 32 bits instead of 4, the control
selects ten operations instead of eight, and the selection is written as a
`case` in `always_comb` instead of a chain of `? :`. The two describe the
same multiplexer, but the `case` stays readable with ten branches. The lab
operations also map onto the core:

| Lab ALU (`alu_control`) | In HIPV |
|---|---|
| addition, subtraction | `ALU_ADD`, `ALU_SUB` |
| bitwise AND, OR, XOR | `ALU_AND`, `ALU_OR`, `ALU_XOR` |
| compare (equal) | `beq`/`bne` in `branchcmp`, not in the ALU |
| pass-through `b` | `lui`: `0 + imm`, through `ALU_ADD` with `SRCA_ZERO` |
| pass-through `a` | not needed |

New in HIPV are the shifts and the signed/unsigned comparisons `slt` and
`sltu`, and these are where the typical mistakes lie. The IEU testbench in
the HIPV repository, `tb/unit/ieu/test_ieu.py`, checks exactly these. Its
first test, `test_alu_ops`, runs all ten operations, including a signed and
an unsigned compare on the same operands and an arithmetic shift of a
negative value. Run it with `make` in `tb/unit/ieu`.
:::

## Jump mechanism

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- `branchcmp`: is the branch condition true? → `TakenE`
- `targetadd`, `targetmux`: where to jump → `PCTargetE`
- `PCSrcE`: do we jump now?
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The last part of the IEU decides whether the program continues
sequentially or jumps. It answers three questions, each with its own block:
is the branch condition true (`branchcmp`), where does the jump go
(`targetadd` and `targetmux`), and should Fetch be redirected now
(`PCSrcE`).
:::

### Conditional branches: `branchcmp`

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
  always_comb
    case (Funct3E)
      3'b000:  TakenE = (A == B);                    // beq
      3'b001:  TakenE = (A != B);                    // bne
      3'b100:  TakenE = ($signed(A) < $signed(B));   // blt
      3'b101:  TakenE = ($signed(A) >= $signed(B));  // bge
      3'b110:  TakenE = (A < B);                     // bltu
      3'b111:  TakenE = (A >= B);                    // bgeu
      default: TakenE = 1'b0;                        // reserved encodings
    endcase
```

- Operands: `FwdAE`, `WriteDataE` (forwarded `rs1`, `rs2`)
- Separate from the ALU: the ALU is free for other work
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The branch comparator evaluates the condition of the six RV32I branches,
selected by `Funct3E`:

```systemverilog
module branchcmp (input  logic [31:0] A, B,
                  input  logic [2:0]  Funct3E,
                  output logic        TakenE);

  always_comb
    case (Funct3E)
      3'b000:  TakenE = (A == B);                    // beq
      3'b001:  TakenE = (A != B);                    // bne
      3'b100:  TakenE = ($signed(A) < $signed(B));   // blt
      3'b101:  TakenE = ($signed(A) >= $signed(B));  // bge
      3'b110:  TakenE = (A < B);                     // bltu
      3'b111:  TakenE = (A >= B);                    // bgeu
      default: TakenE = 1'b0;                        // reserved encodings
    endcase

endmodule
```

It is connected to the forwarded register operands, not to the ALU
operands:

```systemverilog
  branchcmp bcmp(.A(FwdAE), .B(WriteDataE), .Funct3E(Funct3E), .TakenE(TakenE));
```

A branch compares two registers, `rs1` and `rs2`, so it needs the same
forwarded values as any other instruction. Many processors compare with the
ALU, by subtracting and checking the result. HIPV uses a separate
comparator, which costs a little more hardware, but keeps the ALU free and
the two jobs independent. `TakenE` is meaningful only for branches. For
every other instruction it is computed from whatever `Funct3E` and the
operands happen to be, and ignored, because `BranchE` is 0.
:::

### Jump targets: `targetadd` and `targetmux`

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
  adder #(32) targetadd(.A(PCE), .B(ImmExtE), .Y(PCTargetBaseE));
  assign JalrTargetE = {ALUResultE[31:1], 1'b0};
  mux2 #(32) targetmux(.D0(PCTargetBaseE), .D1(JalrTargetE), .S(JalrE), .Y(PCTargetE));
```

| Instruction | Target | Computed by |
|---|---|---|
| `beq` … `bgeu`, `jal` | `PC + imm` | `targetadd` |
| `jalr` | `(rs1 + imm) & ~1` | ALU, bit 0 cleared |
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
RV32I has two kinds of targets. Branches and `jal` are **PC-relative**:
the target is the address of the instruction plus the immediate. `jalr` is
**register-relative**: the target is `rs1 + imm`, which is how a function
returns (`jalr x0, 0(x1)`, written `ret`) and how a program jumps through a
table of addresses.

```systemverilog
  // branch/jump target: PC + imm for branch/jal, ALU (rs1 + imm) for jalr
  adder #(32) targetadd(.A(PCE), .B(ImmExtE), .Y(PCTargetBaseE));
  assign JalrTargetE = {ALUResultE[31:1], 1'b0};
  mux2 #(32) targetmux(.D0(PCTargetBaseE), .D1(JalrTargetE), .S(JalrE), .Y(PCTargetE));
```

The PC-relative target has its own adder, `targetadd`, the same generic
`adder` that increments the PC in the IFU. The register-relative target
needs no new hardware: for `jalr`, Decode sets up the ALU to compute
`rs1 + imm`, as for a load. The ISA requires the lowest bit of the `jalr`
target to be cleared, which costs nothing in hardware, only wiring:
`{ALUResultE[31:1], 1'b0}`. The multiplexer `targetmux` then selects the
ALU path for `jalr` and the adder for everything else.

The ALU result of a `jal` or `jalr` is not what the instruction writes to
its destination register. Both write the return address, `PC + 4`, which
is why `PCPlus4E` travels on to Writeback with them.
:::

### The redirect: `PCSrcE`

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
  assign PCSrcE = ValidEReg & ReadyM & (JumpE | JalrE | (BranchE & TakenE));
```

- Jump: always; branch: only if `TakenE`
- `ValidEReg`: a bubble never redirects
- `ReadyM`: only in the cycle the instruction **leaves** Execute
  - one-cycle pulse
  - while it waits, its forwarded operands may not be ready
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The last line of the IEU decides whether to redirect:

```systemverilog
  // redirect, qualified with the valid bit and gated to the retire cycle
  assign PCSrcE = ValidEReg & ReadyM & (JumpE | JalrE | (BranchE & TakenE));
```

The term in parentheses is the RV32I rule: a jump (`jal`, `jalr`) always
changes the PC, a branch only if its condition is true. The two qualifiers
in front make it safe in the elastic pipeline:

- **`ValidEReg`**: a bubble must never redirect. When the stage is empty,
  its pipeline registers still hold the controls of the last instruction,
  and without the valid bit an old branch could fire a second time.
- **`ReadyM`**: the redirect fires only in the cycle in which the
  instruction leaves Execute. This has two reasons. First, it makes
  `PCSrcE` a one-cycle pulse, which is what the IFU expects. Second, while
  the instruction waits, its operands may not be final. A branch that
  depends on a load still in the Memory stage compares garbage until the
  data arrives. The refresh loop will correct its operands, but a redirect
  issued from the garbage could not be taken back. Waiting for `ReadyM`
  means the branch decides only with its final operands.

Note what does *not* happen: the branch itself is not flushed. It leaves
Execute normally at the same edge, and the redirect removes only the
instructions behind it, in Fetch and Decode.
:::

## Summary

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- Four parts: handshake + registers, forwarding, ALU, jump mechanism
- Built from generic blocks; only `alu` and `branchcmp` are behavioral
- Forwarding: `mux3` per operand, selected by the hazard unit
- Refresh loop: `HoldE` keeps forwarded values while the stage waits
- `PCSrcE` fires once, when a valid branch or jump leaves Execute
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The IEU executes every RV32I instruction in a single cycle. Like the IFU,
most of it is structural, built from `flopenr`, `mux2`, `mux3` and `adder`.
Only the two leaf cells that compute, the ALU and the branch comparator,
are behavioral.

Its four parts follow the flow of an instruction. The handshake logic and
the D/E pipeline registers accept the instruction from Decode and hold it
while it waits. The forwarding multiplexers replace out-of-date register
operands with newer values from the Memory and Writeback stages, and the
refresh loop keeps those values in the operand registers when the stage
stalls, so that a forwarded value is never lost. The ALU computes the
result, or the address of a load or store. The jump mechanism compares the
branch operands, computes the target, and redirects Fetch exactly once, in
the cycle a taken branch or jump leaves Execute.
:::
